history.text: Scholarly debate: 'Celtoscepticism' (e.g. John Collis) rejects applying ethnic 'Celtic' labels to archaeological material such as La Tène artefacts, noting ancient writers did not call Irish or British peoples Celts; many scholars now treat 'Celtic' primarily as a linguistic category.
history.label: evidence (from abstracts/summaries; full texts not read)

history.text: Irish archaeology has largely moved away from a prehistoric 'Celtic invasion' model; the Iron Age shows continuity and regional identities.
history.label: evidence (abstract-level)

history.text: Irish myths were transmitted orally then written down by Christian scribes in the early medieval period.
history.label: evidence

history.text: The Royal Sites (Cashel, Dún Ailinne, Uisneach, Rathcroghan, Tara, plus Navan Fort/Emain Macha in NI) were sites of royal inauguration, ceremony and assembly for the provinces; Tara was seat of the kings of Meath and the high kings.
history.label: evidence

history.text: The Royal Sites are described as large-scale Iron Age complexes with roots in the Neolithic, linked to myth and to the transition to Christianity and St Patrick.
history.label: evidence

history.text: County Sligo holds about one hundred interconnected passage-tomb sites (Carrowmore and Carrowkeel foci, 23 km apart), infused with medieval Gaelic myth.
history.label: evidence

history.text: Lug's roots can be traced to the Gaulish god Lugos, whom Caesar equated with Mercury.
history.label: evidence

cycles.text: The four-cycle division (Mythological, Ulster, Fenian, Kings/Historical) is a modern (19th-century) scholarly scheme; medieval compilers instead classified tales by title type (e.g. Táin = cattle raid).
cycles.label: evidence

cycles.text: Mythological Cycle: Tuatha Dé Danann, Fomorians and legendary invasions; key texts Lebor Gabála Érenn, Cath Maige Tuired, Tochmarc Étaíne, and two of the 'Three Sorrows of Storytelling' (Children of Tuireann; Children of Lir). Hero Lug Lámfhota; leader Nuadu Airgetlám.
cycles.label: evidence
cycles.name: Mythological Cycle

cycles.text: Ulster Cycle (earlier 'Red Branch'): centred on Cú Chulainn, King Conchobar and the Táin Bó Cúailnge, in which Medb of Connacht seeks the Donn Cuailnge (Brown Bull); includes Deirdre, the third Sorrow.
cycles.label: evidence
cycles.name: Ulster Cycle

cycles.text: Fenian (Fianna/Ossianic) Cycle: Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna; strong links to Gaelic Scotland.
cycles.label: evidence
cycles.name: Fenian Cycle

cycles.text: Cycle of the Kings (Historical Cycle): tales of mythical, semi-historical and historical kings, roughly 3rd c. BC to 8th c. AD per UNC pathfinder.
cycles.label: evidence
cycles.name: Cycle of the Kings

cycles.text: Three Sorrows of Storytelling: Children of Tuireann and Children of Lir (Mythological Cycle) and Deirdre (Ulster Cycle).
cycles.label: evidence

cycles.text: In the Children of Lir, Aoife turns the children into swans at Loch Dairbhreach; they spend 300 years each at Loch Dairbhreach, Sruth na Maoile and Iorrus Domnann/Inis Gluairé.
cycles.label: evidence

places.text: Brú na Bóinne (Knowth, Newgrange, Dowth) - Neolithic passage-tomb landscape on a bend of the River Boyne about 40 km north of Dublin; UNESCO 1993.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Sceilg Mhichíl (Skellig Michael) - early medieval island monastery ~12 km off the Iveragh Peninsula, Co. Kerry; UNESCO 1996.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Emain Macha (Co. Armagh) and the Hill of Tara (Co. Meath) are settings of the Ulster Cycle.
places.label: evidence

places.label: evidence

places.label: inference

places.text: Newgrange Passage Tomb (Megalithic tomb - passage tomb, Co. Meath): The great passage tomb mound of Newgrange built over 5,000 years ago during the middle of the Neolithic period (around 3200 BC) is one of a number of monuments which, together with the nearby passage tombs of Knowth and Dowth, form part of the ‘Brú na Bóinne’ UNESCO World Heritage Site.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Knowth Passage Tomb Cemetery (Megalithic tomb - passage tomb, Co. Meath): The great passage tomb cemetery of Knowth, built over 5,000 years ago during the middle of the Neolithic period (around 3200 BC), is one of a number of monuments which, together with the nearby passage tombs of Newgrange and Dowth, form part of ‘Brú na Bóinne’ UNESCO World Heritage Site.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Hill of Tara (Graveyard, Co. Meath): Though best known as the seat of the High Kings of Ireland, the Hill of Tara has been an important site since the late Stone Age when a passage-tomb was constructed there.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Hill of Uisneach (Barrow - pond barrow, Co. Westmeath): A range of archaeological monuments on The Hill of Uisneach including ‘Lough Lugh’ marks the mythological and sacred centre of prehistoric Ireland, in modern day County Westmeath.  This ancient assembly site can be compared to other Royal centres in prehistoric Ireland including the Hill of Tara in Co.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Rathcroghan (Mound, Co. Roscommon): Hidden within the tranquil scenery of North Co.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Loughcrew Megalithic Cemetery (Megalithic tomb - passage tomb, Co. Meath): The Loughcrew Cairns, also known as the Hills of the Witch, are a group of Neolithic passage tombs dating to 3000 BC.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Carrowmore Megalithic Cemetery (Megalithic tomb - passage tomb, Co. Sligo): This is the largest cemetery of megalithic tombs in Ireland and is also among the country's oldest, with monuments ranging from five and a half thousand to six and a half thousand years old.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Rock of Cashel (Cathedral, Co. Tipperary South): A spectacular group of Medieval buildings set on an outcrop of limestone in the Golden Vale including the 12th century round tower, High Cross and Romanesque Chapel, 13th century Gothic cathedral, 15th century Castle and the restored Hall of the Vicars Choral.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Dún Aonghasa (Cliff-edge fort, Co. Galway): Perched spectacularly on a cliff overlooking the Atlantic ocean, this is the largest of the prehistoric stone forts of the Aran Islands.
places.label: evidence

places.text: The 'Grianán of Aileach' (Hillfort, Co. Donegal): On the summit of Greenan Mountain is the stone fort known as the Grianán of Aileach.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Céide Fields (Field system, Co. Mayo): Beneath the wild boglands of North Mayo lies the Céide Fields, the most extensive Stone Age monument in the world, consisting of field systems, dwelling areas and megalithic tombs.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Corlea Trackway (Road - class 1 togher, Co. Longford): The centre interprets an Iron Age bog road that was built in the year 148 B.C.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Drombeg Stone Circle (Stone circle - multiple-stone, Co. Cork): Drombeg stone circle is dramatically situated on a rocky terrace with sweeping views over farmland to the Atlantic Ocean.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Proleek Megalithic Tombs (Megalithic tomb - portal tomb, Co. Louth): Located to the south-west of the Cooley Mountains near the lower slopes of Black Mountain, Proleek portal tomb is one of the best-known and most iconic megalithic tombs in Ireland.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Browneshill Megalithic Tomb (Megalithic tomb - portal tomb, Co. Carlow): Known as the ‘Browneshill dolmen’, because it is sited on a hill on which sits the former estate house of the Browne family, the remains of this megalithic tomb are well-preserved and the chamber faces down slope to the east.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Clonmacnoise (Graveyard, Co. Offaly): An Early Christian site founded by St.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Glendalough (Graveyard, Co. Wicklow): This early Christian ecclesiastical settlement was founded by St.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Skellig Michael (Terrace, Co. Kerry): The magnificent Skellig Islands lie 8 miles (12 km) off the coast of Portmagee in South West Kerry.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Reask Monastic Site (Ecclesiastical enclosure, Co. Kerry): Nothing is known about the history of the ancient church site at Reask situated on the spectacular Dingle Peninsula.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Fore (Religious house - Benedictine monks, Co. Westmeath): Fore is situated in a marshy valley and takes its name from the Irish word fobhair, meaning a spring or a well.
places.label: evidence

places.text: Mellifont Abbey (Religious house - Cistercian monks, Co. Louth): The first Cistercian monastery in Ireland founded in 1142 by St Malachy of Armagh, its most unusual feature is the octagonal Lavabo c.
places.label: evidence
